clue.text: Trouble has engulfed the prince of Abyssinia

indicators.note: to engulf is to swallow up, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: taken as written
Ras is the Ethiopian title for a prince or chief

explanation.surface: Unrest has swallowed up an Ethiopian prince.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' gives its own letters and 'engulfed' puts RAS inside it. Abyssinia is the old name for Ethiopia, where Ras was a princely title (as in Ras Tafari).
explanation.definitionFit: To harass is to pester and torment, a synonym of the verb trouble.

clue.text: He serves in a French lake island

parts.note: lac is the French word for lake
a key or cay is a low island, as in the Florida Keys

explanation.surface: A waiter works on an island in a French lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A lackey is a servant or footman, so a man who waits on others.

clue.text: Long-distance communication by a trumpeter?

parts.note: the trumpeter is an elephant, and the old term for a long-distance telephone call names its nose

explanation.walkthrough: The held text has a stray '7' the scan does not print. Elephants trumpet through their trunks, and a long-distance phone call was once so called in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The old British term for a long-distance telephone call, read as the noise made through an elephant's nose.

clue.text: Prosaic submission to the jury

explanation.surface: A dull question is put to the jurors.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosaic means unemotional and practical; in law, a question of fact (not law) is the kind decided by a jury.

clue.text: To lead in France calls for self-possession

parts.note: the French for 'to' is a, the 'in France' covering both pieces
the French name for the heavy grey metal, the same root as the plumber's plumb line

explanation.surface: Someone taking charge in France will need to keep their cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'calls for' is only a link. Both pieces are French: a (to) and plomb (lead), giving the phrase 'à plomb', literally 'plumb upright'.
explanation.definitionFit: Poise and calm confidence under pressure is what the word describes.

clue.text: Father turns up an article in the Pacific

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for father

indicators.note: to turn is to face the other way, so the next word is read backwards

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Dad pops up with an item somewhere in the Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' looks like 'arrives' but 'turns' reverses UP to give PU.
explanation.definitionFit: Papua is the southern part of New Guinea, an island in the western Pacific Ocean.

clue.text: Original moves on board

parts.note: the first moves of a chess game, which have named sequences

explanation.walkthrough: 'board' is a chessboard: the standard first moves of a game have this name.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the named first sequences of play are these, the moves that begin a game.

clue.text: High-born lady one's seen in places of refreshment

indicators.note: something seen within a place is put inside it

parts.note: bars are places serving drinks
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A noblewoman is spotted in pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A baroness is a woman of noble rank, the female counterpart of a baron.

clue.text: Tells about continental aristocracy

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word for 'concerning'
counts are European noblemen, the continental equivalent of British earls

explanation.surface: A gossip passes on stories about European nobility.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount a story is to narrate it, so both verbs mean relates.

clue.text: A soft fruit, it would seem

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for soft
a pear is a common orchard fruit

explanation.surface: Something seems to be a ripe piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text drops the opening 'A', which the scan prints and the wordplay needs. 'it would' is surface padding: 'it would appear' and 'it would seem' are the same idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: To appear and to seem are synonyms, both meaning to give an impression.

clue.text: Rest on the island ? Legally he's got it coming to him

definitions.text: Legally he's got it coming to him

parts.note: the remainder is what is left, the rest
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: Someone resting on an island is told he has an inheritance on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' joins the pieces. A remainderman is the legal term for one who inherits an estate once an earlier interest ends.
explanation.definitionFit: In property law this is the person entitled to an estate after a prior interest expires.

clue.text: Takes minced meat

indicators.note: minced meat is chopped up, so the letters of the neighbouring word are chopped and rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'minced' looks like part of the meat description but signals the anagram of TAKES.
explanation.definitionFit: A steak is a thick slice of beef, an example of meat.

clue.text: Side-view of a lift perhaps ?

explanation.surface: An architect's drawing shows a lift from one side.
explanation.definitionFit: An architect's side drawing of a building is so named, and raising something up, a lift, is also called that.

clue.text: Bachelor Doyle meets D. Roe for breakfast

parts.note: BA is the degree Bachelor of Arts
Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes
roe is the mass of eggs of a fish

explanation.surface: A single man named Doyle has a meeting with a D. Roe over the morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'D. Roe' reads as a person's name but splits into the letter D and roe, fish eggs. 'meets' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Fried bacon with eggs is the traditional cooked British morning meal.

clue.text: How can the Scots dare to wear it ?

definitions.text: How can the Scots dare to wear it ?

indicators.note: asking how the letters can be made into something signals that they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Scotsmen in kilts are asked how they would dare to wear formal tails.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of SCOTS DARE rearrange into the answer, and the whole clue asks how Scots in their kilts could bring themselves to wear the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal tailcoat worn for evening dress.

clue.text: Not the type to strike one as a bluestocking?

definitions.text: Not the type to strike one as a bluestocking?

parts.words: Not the type to strike one as a bluestocking?
parts.note: plays on 'strike' as an industrial walkout and on leg colour: a bluestocking is a learned woman

explanation.walkthrough: One who refuses to join a strike is so called; the clue pairs 'black' with 'blue' and 'leg' with 'stocking'.
explanation.definitionFit: A strike-breaker, a worker who keeps working while colleagues are on strike.

clue.text: Let's ring the changes in currency

indicators.note: ringing the changes means trying the different orders, so these letters are re-ordered

explanation.surface: Bell-ringers propose to ring peals in exchange for money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring the changes' is a bell-ringing phrase; 'ring' is part of the fodder LETS RING, and 'the changes' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterling is the British pound, the UK's money.

clue.text: Always on hand, but uncommonly thick for Rehoboam?

definitions.text: Always on hand, but uncommonly thick for Rehoboam?

parts.words: Always on hand, but uncommonly thick for Rehoboam?
parts.note: a digit always on the hand; King Rehoboam boasted in 1 Kings 12 that his smallest digit would be thicker than his father's loins

explanation.walkthrough: In the Bible, Rehoboam tells his people 'My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins', so for him this smallest digit was unusually thick.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest digit on a hand, which Rehoboam claimed was thicker than his father's waist.

clue.text: Was this gift-horse so lacking in vitality ?

definitions.text: Was this gift-horse so lacking in vitality ?

parts.words: Was this gift-horse so lacking in vitality ?
parts.note: the Trojan horse, a gift to Troy, was made of timber, and a stiff lifeless performance is described with the same word

explanation.walkthrough: The Greeks' gift-horse at Troy was built of timber; the adjective for 'made of timber' also means stiff and lifeless.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means made of timber and also stiff and expressionless.

clue.text: " Can this cockpit hold The vasty fields of ----- ?" (Henry V)

definitions.text: " Can this cockpit hold The vasty fields of ----- ?" (Henry V)

parts.words: " Can this cockpit hold The vasty fields of ----- ?" (Henry V)
parts.note: a quotation from the Prologue of Shakespeare's Henry V, where the Chorus asks if the theatre can hold the battlefields of England's enemy

explanation.walkthrough: In the Prologue to Henry V, the Chorus asks whether a small theatre can hold the battlefields of the country Henry invades, scene of Agincourt.
explanation.definitionFit: The country where Henry V fought at Agincourt fills the blank in the Chorus's line.

clue.text: Long-lasting, the French story

parts.note: a chronic illness is one that persists for a long time
le is the French masculine definite article

explanation.surface: A French tale that goes on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicle is a historical account of events, a kind of narrative.

clue.text: Girl seeking plume ?

parts.note: plays on the classic French-lesson phrase 'la plume de ma tante', the pen of my aunt

explanation.walkthrough: 'plume' is French for pen; the phrase-book sentence 'la plume de ma tante' (my aunt's pen) is what an aunt's relative would go looking for.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter, the girl whose aunt owns the famous pen.

clue.text: Track sport is never-ending — nothing in it!

indicators.note: the nothing is placed inside the shortened sport
a word with no ending loses its final letter, so the last letter of sport goes

parts.note: taken as written before trimming
O, the figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: An athletics event goes on forever with nothing happening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'never-ending' cuts SPORT to SPOR, and 'in it' puts O inside to make SPOOR. 'Track' looks like a running track but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoor is the trail of footprints or droppings left by an animal.

clue.text: Hang about intentionally ?

parts.note: refers to the old English legal offence of lingering 'with intent' to commit a crime

explanation.walkthrough: The British offence 'loitering with intent', used under the old 'sus' laws, makes hanging about intentionally a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: To linger idly is the plain sense; the legal phrase adds the intention.

clue.text: Turn me blonde for a change, to put me in good heart

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

clue.text: Choked when forced to shut up

explanation.surface: Someone retched when they were silenced by force.
explanation.definitionFit: To gag is to retch or choke, and also to silence someone by stopping their mouth.

clue.text: Cite an example
